name: Grasping at own-nature (inherent existence)
description: Taking things born of causes and conditions as existing by their own nature; the root of views, disputes and afflictions and, as ignorance, of the twelve links.

name: Taking emptiness as a view
description: Holding emptiness itself as a thesis or entity; the Victors called those who do so incurable, like a patient in whom the medicine itself stays unexpelled.
antidotes: cpt:emptiness-of-emptiness (understanding that emptiness too is empty)

name: Misreading emptiness as nothingness
description: Taking emptiness to mean that nothing exists, so that karma, the path and the Buddha are denied; wrongly seen emptiness destroys the slow-witted like a snake wrongly grasped.

name: The two extremes: eternalism and annihilationism
description: 'It is' is the grasp of permanence and 'it is not' the view of annihilation; whoever accepts real existents falls into one or the other.
antidotes: the middle way of dependent origination

name: The view of the transitory collection
description: The view that takes the aggregates as 'I' and 'mine', from which all afflictions and faults arise.

equivalents.note: the same view named in Pali; the first of the fetters

name: Conceptual elaboration (prapañca)
description: Verbal-conceptual elaboration from which conceptual construction, action and afflictions arise; those who elaborate the Buddha do not see him.

equivalents.note: Pali papañca in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta is proliferation rooted in craving, conceit and views

name: The four errors
description: Taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure and the selfless as self; the afflictions arise in dependence on them.
antidotes: contemplation of impermanence, suffering, impurity and selflessness (CŚ 1–4)

name: 'I'-making and 'mine'-making
description: Grasping at 'I' and 'mine', which arises from grasping at the aggregates and brings action and birth; its ceasing ends grasping and birth.

name: Grasping at nirvāṇa
description: The thought 'without grasping I shall attain nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa will be mine' is itself a great grasping.

name: The obscurations of afflictions and of the knowable
description: The obscuration of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa), which prevents liberation, and the obscuration of the knowable (jñeyāvaraṇa), which prevents omniscience; emptiness is the antidote to both.

name: Anger (dveṣa, pratigha)
description: Anger destroys the merit accumulated over thousands of aeons; there is no evil equal to hatred.

name: Self-cherishing (desiring one's own happiness)
description: All who suffer in the world suffer from desiring their own happiness; all calamities and fears come from grasping at self.

name: Laziness and its kinds
description: The opposite of vigour: laziness, attachment to what is base, and despondency with self-contempt.

name: Laxity and excitement, and the other faults of concentration
description: The faults of concentration: laziness, forgetting the object, laxity and excitement, non-application and over-application, remedied by the eight factors.

name: Mere non-thought mistaken for wisdom
description: Cultivating the mere absence of recollection and attention without correct analysis; like fainting, it only cultivates delusion and cannot remove the obscurations.

name: The eight worldly concerns
description: Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, which the wise treat as equal.
